$comment: Repos where Sparkle will NEVER merge on its own authority, no matter what any config says.
THIS FILE IS A TEST FIXTURE. IT IS NOT READ AT RUNTIME, AND MUST NEVER BE.
Read that twice before wiring anything to it. `apps/desktop/shared/` is NOT in
tauri.conf.json's `bundle.resources` (only `resources/*.mjs|js` and the roborev hooks are), so
a `std::fs::read_to_string` or a bundler import of this path RESOLVES IN THE DEV TREE AND FAILS
IN THE SHIPPED DMG. That failure is silent and it fails OPEN: no pinned slugs means no `deny`
floor, so the exact repos this file exists to protect become mergeable in the packaged app while
every test stays green — because the tests read this file from the repo, where it is always
present. A fail-open security floor that is invisible to its own test suite is the worst
outcome available here, so the runtime read is forbidden rather than merely discouraged.
HOW IT IS ACTUALLY USED. Each side declares its OWN hand-written constant — `MERGE_PROTECTED_SLUGS`
in `services/conciergeTools/policy.ts`, and its twin in Rust — and each side's TEST reads this
file from disk and asserts its constant matches. The list is therefore compiled into the build as
a constant; this JSON is only what stops the two copies drifting apart. That is exactly the
arrangement `destructive-commands.json` uses for the deny rules, whose comment is careful to say
it is read by both halves' TEST SUITES — a qualifier an earlier version of this header dropped,
which is how the runtime-read reading became available at all.
THE PROBLEM THE LIST SOLVES. Concierge tool tiers used to be ONE GLOBAL TIER: `merge_pr` was
allow / ask / deny for every project at once. The owner of this machine holds commit access to
repos he does NOT own, and his standing rule there is that no PR merges without a human. With a
single global tier those two facts conflict, and the conflict was being resolved by pinning the
GLOBAL tier to `ask` — i.e. interrupting him for every merge in his own repo in order to protect
a repo he does not own.
WHY A PINNED LIST RATHER THAN A CONFIG ENTRY. `[concierge.projects."<slug>".tools]` in the
user's config.toml expresses the same thing and is the general mechanism — but it lives in a
file, and a file can be reset, hand-edited, or superseded by a future change to the shipped
defaults. The whole ask was that the rule survive WITHOUT anyone remembering it. So these slugs
are a FLOOR: config can tighten past them and can never loosen them.
SLUG SHAPE IS ASSERTED, NOT MERELY DESCRIBED. Entries are GitHub `owner/repo`, lowercase, no
surrounding whitespace and no URL prefix. That invariant fails OPEN if violated — a hand-edited
`Plow-PBC/tkmx-web` would never match a lowercased incoming slug, so that repo would silently
lose its pin while the anti-drift tests stayed green (all three copies would agree on the
mis-cased string). So each side's pin test also asserts the SHAPE of every entry and that the
list is non-empty, rather than trusting this paragraph.
